title: Bethlehem, read slowly (Luke 2:1–20)
hookLine: Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart

cards: Plastic figures on a lawn. A school play with a kid in a bathrobe. A stable, an innkeeper, an ox and a donkey, a star.
Forget the nativity set for a moment, and read only what Luke actually wrote. It's twenty verses, and it starts not with angels but with an emperor.
A decree goes out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be enrolled, and Joseph goes up from Nazareth to Bethlehem, the city of David, with Mary, who is with child.

teach.b: Then one sentence, in the Douay-Rheims: "And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him up in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn." That's all.

No innkeeper; Luke never mentions one. No ox and donkey; later tradition brought them in from a line in Isaiah, and Saint Francis had a living ox and donkey beside his crib at Greccio. Even inn may be the wrong picture.

Luke's Greek word, kataluma, can mean a guest room; it's the word he later uses for the upper room of the Last Supper. So it may have been a crowded family house, with the baby laid where the animals ate.
A manger is a feeding trough. And Bethlehem, read as Hebrew, is beit lechem: house of bread.

teach.h: A FEEDING TROUGH IN THE HOUSE OF BREAD.
teach.b: Some Catholic preachers draw a line from there: the child laid in a feeding trough in the house of bread is the one Catholics receive as the bread of life.
Then shepherds at night with their flocks, an angel, their fear, and good news of great joy.

teach.h: GLORY TO GOD IN THE HIGHEST.
teach.b: A multitude sings: "Glory to God in the highest; and on earth peace to men of good will." The Gloria at Mass begins with those words. The shepherds find it just as they were told, and tell everyone, and everyone wonders.
Then the quietest line in the chapter: "But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart." Pondering translates symballousa, putting things together, setting pieces side by side.
Luke doesn't say she understood it all. She kept it, and turned it over.

how: Catholics hear Luke 2:1–20 at the Christmas Masses at night and at dawn, sing the angels' words in the Gloria at Sunday Mass, and set up a crèche in homes and churches, a custom often traced to Saint Francis.

o: house of bread, the town of David
place of shepherds, a village of the plains
city of peace, the holy city of the kings

games.q: Bethlehem, read slowly — tap the pairs.

s: Luke mentions an innkeeper who turned them away
there's no innkeeper anywhere in Luke. only that there was no room in the kataluma.
the ox and donkey are in Luke's account
later tradition brought them in from Isaiah 1:3; Francis put a living pair at Greccio.
the Gloria at Mass begins with the angels' words from Luke 2
glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace.

games.q: you're Mary. shepherds burst in at night, telling of angels and a sky full of song about your baby. everyone is amazed. what do you do?
o: tell everyone you knew all along.
keep these words, and ponder them in your heart.
games.why: "Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart." not explaining, but keeping, and turning them over.

practice: Let one thing come up that you haven't figured out yet: something someone said years ago that still comes back, a moment that felt holy and you never told anyone, a hard thing you don't understand.
Don't solve it; hold it, turn it over, and set it beside other things you know, the way Mary did. If you pray, ponder it with God.

wordCard.voice: Bethlehem. The city of David, whose name means house of bread, where Mary laid her firstborn son in a manger. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: Bethlehem, house of bread, the town of David.

carryVoice: Your line: she kept all these things. Not solved, just kept, and turned over. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him up in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn.
Glory to God in the highest; and on earth peace to men of good will.
But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart.
